    <id>https://blog.curiousquail.com/the-racism-in-the-redwall-books-sure-is-fascinating/</id>
    <title>The Racism in the Redwall Books Sure Is Fascinating</title>
    <updated>2026-08-10T00:19:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>curiousquail</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;!-- header above --&gt;
&lt;div style="text-align: justify;"&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;b&gt;Visiting a beloved children's franchise late in life has been a trip&lt;/b&gt;
&lt;br&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/xmpns5mcu4b1juhefxpgw/MK3_7550.jpg?rlkey=z8np934cgjlus1oek56x7vjpn&amp;raw=1" target="new"&gt;
&lt;img height="1400" width="2100" alt="Three books stacked on top of each other on a wooden table; the top one is 'Outcast of Redwall' by Brian Jacques and features a ferret-like creature peering through bushes" title=" " src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/curiousquail/mk3_7550_web.jpg"&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Sometime around last summer I started reading the Redwall books with my kids; I've known a lot of people who'd read them growing up or for whom those books meant a lot but they'd missed me entirely until the year of our Abbot 2025 and so I'm coming at this from a probably more critical lens than the one expected of the target audience from the 90's but man,&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;h3&gt;These mice sure are fucking racist lmao&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;div class="infobox-frame"&gt;
&lt;div class="infobox-icon"&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;div class="infobox-text"&gt;Everything I've got to say here will try to be spoiler free for the franchise, but also keeping in mind I'm only up to the 9th book (&lt;i&gt;Pearls of Lutra&lt;/i&gt;, 1996) so there could be additional context I'm missing going forward. Also I'm using the term 'racist' in terms of in-universe xenophobia toward different species but also the real-world analogs of how some of the species are written&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;div style="text-align: justify;"&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If you, like me, have somehow missed out on this franchise - the premise of the first book is pretty straightforward; low fantasy Europe where animals are confusingly anthropomorphized into people but also depicted as animals simultaneously; there's hints that humans (and Portugal!) exist but that's quickly dropped by the second book and never commented upon again, so instead of a NIMH or Warriors type situation where the creatures live as creatures and hide, they like...have jobs and houses and fishing vessels. It's pretty wild. I don't go here but it's like a third thing, a mid-point between NIMH and furry basically.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Anyway, a group of mice have built a big-ass Abbey out of red stone that while not &lt;em&gt;religious&lt;/em&gt;, features an order that's centered around the memory of a "Warrior mouse" from ages ago. They tend to crops, help the sick, take care of an &lt;em&gt;alarming&lt;/em&gt; number of orphans (that seem to have no official source), cook more food than is reasonable&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; and occasionally fend off their territory from invaders.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The books are pretty line-in-the-sand clear on the "good" animals being mice (and to a lesser extent voles) who are depicted as "good honest English folk", moles being their labor force that are incomprehensible simpletons with like, Welsh or Summserset accents (written phonetically&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-2"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-2"&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;!!), hedgehogs written as either Scottish or maybe Mancunian beermakers, otters being depicted as effectively Irish sailors, and shrews showing up regularly as a "so we needed an army to come in an mop up the bad'uns" plot device (while also a parody of how unionized workforces apparently argue all the time? Not sure what is point was trying to be with the whole "Union of Shrews" thing).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Badgers play confusing gendered roles as the books go on because the females are all written like horrific southern mammy stereotypes who not only are in charge of the orphans but also are regularly physically abusive to them, and the males are warrior lords who abandon their families in pursuit of honor and often go berserk, killing friend and foe alike when hit with "the bloodwrath". There's also rabbits who are almost always in military adjacent roles and speak like 1940's RAF pilot stereotypes: "'bout that time, don'cha know chaps, wot wot". It's a little jarring lmao.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;These are all, again, ostensibly the "good guys".&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The "bad" animals are all "vermin", you see. Rats primarily, with weasels, stoats, ferrets, foxes (including two pine martens to date) as either "invasive warrior hordes" or "lowlife seascum pirates". They always speak either with a cockney British accent or in stereotypical "pirate dialect". Ahoy, avast, messmate, etc etc - and almost every primary "vermin" antagonist is depicted as having either some kind of disfigurement or physical disability.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Every book so far with few exceptions follows some primary character from the Abbey faction (usually a mouse) at a various point in an ongoing timeline&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-3"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-3"&gt;3&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; where some adventure happens in or around the Abbey; most often, the Abbey itself is threatened by "vermin" in some way and has to be defended by these peace-loving creatures, with the protagonist mouse being at the center and guided by visions from the ancient warrior mouse via like, the ghost parade or some shit.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In some rare cases, the Abbey dwellers open their hearts to a "vermin" character; one wounded, or left behind by their comrades, or a roving band of performers - etc, and &lt;em&gt;every time&lt;/em&gt; the books prove them correct to have been mistrustful of these "evil" creatures. Again, nine books in and we've had &lt;em&gt;one&lt;/em&gt; sympathetic rat...ever?? and they are only forgiven because they turned from their life of "evil" and helped save some orphans. Most "vermin" aren't given any grace, and the books go at length to show how they're more or less all press-ganged into the barbarian hordes or pirate life with no other choices which makes me wonder why we try to garner sympathy from the reader before stating why it's ok they were killed.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When trying to pin down why "vermin" are evil you might automatically assume (as I did when hitting the second book and the main villain is a Cat who rules the kingdom like a despot) that the threat to the Abbey dwellers is being eaten - but by anthropomorphizing the animals (again, more so as the books go on) there's effectively never an existential threat of rats or stoats like, canibalizing the mice. The foxes border on this early on but it's kind of dropped so the "vermin" are usually just unruly barbarians or pirates who want to steal plunder and baked goods or add to their slave labor force.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/tst1wa4l27uhutlulq4ly/MK3_7562.jpg?rlkey=nc0h0sr6vzv1vq1y7iewibyb9&amp;raw=1" target="new"&gt;
&lt;img height="1400" width="2100" alt="Photo of a black and white cat resting on a wooden floor next to the base of a golden dancing pole" title=" " src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/curiousquail/mk3_7562_web.jpg"&gt;&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;small&gt;&lt;i&gt;Mastodon would never hurt the Redwall mice, he's too tired from practicing his pole routine&lt;/i&gt;&lt;/small&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Sapient birds and snakes also feature into the setting with the former being a mixed bag of "these birds are good!" (Owls, despite them absolutely IRL being mouse predators and that being incongruous) and "these birds are bad" (Crows, ravens, y'know...the black birds, y'know, side eye forever), with the latter being an actual "they're going to eat us" threat.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I get that I'm coming to a children's book series about animal people from the 90's with the lens of the mid 2020's and a background in racial studies but it's frankly &lt;em&gt;astounding&lt;/em&gt; how each book gets my hopes up that this time we'll get some justice for the stereotypes we're putting on the non-Abbey creatures, and each time I'm fucking Lucy Footballed with some "it's in their nature, they couldn't help it" Clinton-era suerpredator line justifying why the evil vermin was evil and why it was ok to kill them, hurt them, mistrust them, betray them, etc.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The book I had the most hope for was book 8 (&lt;em&gt;Outcast of Redwall&lt;/em&gt;, 1995) which from title alone could imply a lot of things. The back of the book synopsis describes a situation where we might see some sort of redemption for 'vermin' OR some comeuppance on the Abbey folk for being so fucking xenophobic all the time... but not only is the back of the book &lt;em&gt;not relevant for over 200 pages&lt;/em&gt;, when it &lt;em&gt;does&lt;/em&gt; become relevant it's even more disappointing than the priors&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-4"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-4"&gt;4&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Book nine, which again, we're in the middle of right now, is not showing any sign of beating the above allegations (Though this book's Badger mother is the least abusive of the franchise so far, so hey - progress!!) but I'm comitted to the long haul of reading the whole franchise.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There's plenty in here I &lt;em&gt;do&lt;/em&gt; like, but it's got huge cactus in the cage vibes basically whenever the word "vermin" is used and that's hard to overcome.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Anyway, thanks for reading. Here are your end-of-post cat photos. Snowapple says good morning to some moving boxes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div style="align-items: stretch; display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; justify-content: space-evenly; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;figure style="display: flex; flex-flow: column; margin: 2px; position: relative; text-decoration: none; width: calc(50% - 4px);"&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/k07jnw326n3t4n1ot3228/MK3_7556.jpg?rlkey=18wkycvzap813vntb532qp31x&amp;amp;raw=1"&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/curiousquail/mk3_7556_web.jpg" alt="Photo of a black cat staring off to the left side of the camera; a large stack, ceiling-high of cardboard boxes is behind him" style="height: 100%; margin: 0px; object-fit: cover; width: 100%;"&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;figure style="display: flex; flex-flow: column; margin: 2px; position: relative; text-decoration: none; width: calc(50% - 4px);"&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/hhrupcae761gfsig1gcbm/MK3_7559.jpg?rlkey=6h97aai9ehhymmnj1f6cq9tfl&amp;amp;raw=1"&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/curiousquail/mk3_7559_web.jpg" alt="The cat has turned and is now staring toward the camera" style="height: 100%; margin: 0px; object-fit: cover; width: 100%;"&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/figure&gt;&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;hr&gt;
&lt;/div&gt; 
&lt;!-- comment box and footer below --&gt;
&lt;script defer src="https://comments.friendsofeggbug.org/comentario.js"&gt;&lt;/script&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;comentario-comments&gt;&lt;/comentario-comments&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;octo-thorpe&gt;blaugust&lt;/octo-thorpe&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;I'd be remiss if I didn't point out that, well - you know the way people make fun of Tolkien for not shutting the fuck up about landscapes? that's Redwall author Brian Jacques and food. There are often &lt;em&gt;entire paragraphs&lt;/em&gt; describing in excruciating detail every main dish, desert, appetizer and drink in the feasts these fucking mice are preparing and it's bonkers. A friend roughly 20 years ago told me it's hard to read these books and not get hungry and shit, I get it now.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-2"&gt;&lt;p&gt;I will say this - if you ever want to practice doing various accents from the British isles, these books serve an great starter guide since everything for effectively everyone but the mice is written phonetically and reading dialog out loud gets you half the way there. I can drop into "mole speech" easily after 9 books lmfao&lt;a href="#fnref-2" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-3"&gt;&lt;p&gt;The first book starts after the Abbey has existed for a long time, but the second prequels before the founding; each sequential book jumps all over the place which, to Jaques' credit, is a fun touch because you'll suddenly read a name you haven't heard in three books and they're mentioning how they died at incredibly old age, but you knew them as a mischievous baby side character in the book they were introduced in. Keeps you guessing on "when" the fuck each story takes place and I really enjoy that.&lt;a href="#fnref-3" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-4"&gt;&lt;p&gt;To those who have read it; I'm using 'relevant' loosely because the back of the book straight up lies about the events. Also, Sunflash and Skarlath's gay romance is probably the strongest this series has &lt;em&gt;ever&lt;/em&gt; been and that plotline being tossed aside in the second half is infuriating&lt;a href="#fnref-4" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://onlinegoddess.net/2026/08/heatwave-no/</id>
    <title>Heatwave No. ???</title>
    <updated>2026-08-09T16:27:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>onlinegoddess</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I think I’ve lost count of how many we’ve had now. When I started writing this, it was 3pm and 30°C (86°F for you folks across the pond). There’s the lightest of breezes, but it’s coming from the south, so no relief to speak of.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;picture&gt;
&lt;source srcset="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4725.webp" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"&gt;
&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4723.webp"&gt;
&lt;/picture&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’ve always loved summer, but this really is too much. The overnight temps are regularly staying in the late teens, which means the bedrooms are mid-20s, though luckily that hasn’t been the case this week. With the high humidity, it’s unbearable.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Upstairs windows are kept open all night, but I need blackout blinds up as I hate being woken by the sun really early. Oh, and the sodding mosquitoes, though thankfully they only appeared for a few days and seem to have buggered off now. I have no idea where they are breeding as everything is so dry, even the local ponds are practically gone.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Next week is supposed to bring 34°C  and 19°C at night. Ugghhh….. Perhaps we should have a last minute getaway. To Iceland.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;picture&gt;
&lt;source srcset="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4726.webp" media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)"&gt;
&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4724.webp"&gt;
&lt;/picture&gt;
&lt;p&gt;July was the driest since records began. Many areas saw no rainfall at all - we only had 10 minutes drizzle here. A hosepipe ban has been in effect since mid-July and we are officially in a drought. Frustrating as we are trying to seed the big garden which is largely dirt after all the brambles and nettles were removed.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;We had a horrible wildfire on the Suffolk coast - the beautiful nature reserve at Dunwich. The historic Coastguard Cottages were thankfully saved from disaster, but acres of heathland with all the wildlife it is home to was lost in a matter of hours.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4156.webp" alt="IMG_4156" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;figcaption&gt;© National Trust Images/Justin Minns&lt;/figcaption&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The hens and tortoise are feeling the heat, so we have been running the sprinkler every day to cool the air and give them soft ground to move on. Animals are exempt from the ban anyway.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The cats are spending most of their day sprawled on the hardwood floors in the house or under bushes, trees and garden furniture when outside. Though Jasper is weird and likes to sleep in the corner of our (carpeted) bedroom, the hottest room in the house.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="bearming-gallery"&gt;
&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4729.webp" alt="IMG_4729" /&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4733.webp" alt="IMG_4733" /&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I decided to bring the parasol over from the big garden patio as we tend to sit out the front of the house most of the time. It’s nice to sit in the shade as I write this.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4736.webp" alt="IMG_4736" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;When the weather eventually turns, I’d like to get the big garden finished - it won’t look great this year, but I’m hoping we’ve done the groundwork for next spring/summer. Husband finally managed to get the gutters cleared thanks to our lovely neighbours lending us a ladder, so we are more than ready for LOTS of rain!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’ve also got some ideas for the awkward space at the side of the house. It’s currently got a rotting wood store and what was clearly a flower bed all on a slope and only about 6 feet wide. I’d like to make a little deck up against the house and we can sip our morning cuppa enjoying the view of the church. The ugly green metal fence needs to be replaced too. All this is probably going to be a spring job though, especially as it will cost a bit of money.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/onlinegoddess/img_4702.webp" alt="IMG_4702" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Roll on autumn, you can’t come quickly enough. Just don’t be a record-breaking one for rain please.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://onlinegoddess.net/2026/08/heatwave-no/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-09T16:27:00+00:00</published>

  <entry>
    <id>https://siobhan.bearblog.dev/tinkering-with-bearcode/</id>
    <title>Tinkering with ʕ•ᴥ•ʔ BearCode</title>
    <updated>2026-08-09T10:56:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>siobhan</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Bearblog has rekindled my love of tinkering. I haven't coded for what feels like millennia; it's been at least a decade since I coded something 'proper' and everything has changed. Back when I first taught myself to code it was PHP includes and CSS was simple. I made graphics in Photoshop and pulled them using includes. Now you can do almost anything in the CSS backend and it is blowing my mind. I feel like such a dinosaur.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I've been playing this morning though, taking inspiration from other Bear's and pottering around on the &lt;a href='https://bear.css.observer/'&gt;playground&lt;/a&gt; to see what I can achieve. I was aiming for an &lt;mark&gt;enchanted forest&lt;/mark&gt; vibe, I'm not sure I've achieved quite what I wanted but it's getting there. I foresee a few more days of fiddling around. I &lt;em&gt;really&lt;/em&gt; wanted to add a little header graphic instead of my simple name as the blog title, but I'm not sure I can achieve that on my little free account...&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Things I hope to achieve:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Add a polaroid effect around any images in posts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Alter the highlighting colour effect to a nice peach&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Add a simple header image above the navigation, and a smaller on in the footer panel&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Add more sections to the front homepage&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Actually add some content to the 'About me' page&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Adapt the Guestbook colouring to compliment the new theme&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://siobhan.bearblog.dev/tinkering-with-bearcode/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-09T10:56:00+00:00</published>

  <entry>
    <id>https://binarydigit.net/enjoying-multiple-blog-platforms/</id>
    <title>Enjoying Multiple Blog Platforms</title>
    <updated>2026-08-09T15:30:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>binarydigit</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;It's always difficult for me to stay on one platform every year because I love to tinker with code. Bear blog has been the best so far because it's SO incredibly customizable that I tinker with my design constantly, and I have a lifetime membership so I can always create and remove websites. I want to keep this domain and website going since I can pull all of my hobbies into one place, and I don't want to have to tell folks to constantly update my RSS feed. So I'll stay here, work on my other site experiments elsewhere, and then can pull in my posts from other sites here eventually. I don't think it's a great idea to duplicate my work everywhere, but I don't really care about SEO or any of the corporate stuff, and would like to keep this home as my archive.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Right now I'm using Pagecord to blog (almost) daily for Blaugust, since it has awesome features like posting from Obsidian with micro.pub API, a really great WYSIWYG editor (the addon for Bear isn't quite the same), and drag-n-drop images with alt text easily. I also love that you can send your blog as a newsletter weekly or piece by piece. I'd love those features for Bear blog.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'm also using Tumblr for my art right now since it's easy for folks to reblog and share it. I had deleted my Tumblr that I had from 2008-2023, but recently joined again because there's no replacement for it (even Mastodon).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I also realize that pulling in the RSS feeds with a script might slow down my homepage to some readers depending on their location, so I want to avoid that eventually. I enjoy having my cbox chatbox so that will stay for now.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Happy blogging 💌&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://binarydigit.net/enjoying-multiple-blog-platforms/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-09T15:30:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://angrybunnyman.com/nine-quick-digression-for-a-bear-customization/</id>
    <title>nine: quick digression for a bear customization. Subtitle: read the $%^#ing manual?</title>
    <updated>2026-08-09T15:39:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>angrybunnyman</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;div class="dynamic-title"&gt;Portrait of an attr(artist)&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;div class="nutrition-widget" id="nutritionWidget"&gt;
  &lt;div class="nutrition-content" id="nutritionContent"&gt;
    &lt;h3&gt;Post Nutrition Label&lt;/h3&gt;
    &lt;ul&gt;
      &lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Content Type:&lt;/strong&gt; Text &lt;/li&gt;
      &lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Read Time:&lt;/strong&gt; 5 min &lt;/li&gt;
      &lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Topics:&lt;/strong&gt; CSS, IndieWeb&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;/ul&gt;
  &lt;/div&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;h2 id=reading-standards-is-how-i-relax&gt;Reading standards is how I relax&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I wanted to fix a little thing that's been bugging me in my Bear theme — the lack of customization in the &lt;code&gt;{{ previous_post }}&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;{{ next_post }}&lt;/code&gt; templates. Visually, they only present the linked "previous" or "next" text.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;However, in my screen reader testing, VoiceOver was reading the title of the post it would be linking to. That meant the title was somewhere in the code.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Sure enough:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
   &lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;class&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;previous-post&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;href&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;/{link to your last post}&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;title&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;{title of your last post}&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;Previous&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;/&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
   &lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;class&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;next-post&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;href&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;/{link to your next post}&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt; &lt;span class="na"&gt;title&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;=&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="s"&gt;&amp;quot;{title of your next post}&amp;quot;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;Next&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;/&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;lt;/&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nt"&gt;p&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;&amp;gt;&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If it's there in the HTML, you can use it. I was pretty sure I could pull it off with JavaScript, but my first move whenever I hit a "does X exist" question in CSS (or HTML [or any other standards spec]) is to go straight to the W3C's module documentation. Turns out there's a whole category of CSS functions built for reaching into other parts of the page while it's being styled, before it ever reaches the user: &lt;a href='https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-5/#value-insert'&gt;Miscellaneous Value Substituting Functions&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And in that section is this function: &lt;a href='https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-5/#attr-notation'&gt;attr()&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That function can represent a named attribute on an element on your page. So if something in your page is reliably structured, CSS can reach in and grab that specific something. CSS is &lt;em&gt;really&lt;/em&gt; good at letting you grab specific parts of a page to manipulate.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=so-heres-how-you-do-it&gt;So here's how you do it&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;The browser doesn't apply your stylesheet to raw text.  It parses all the HTML first and builds a structured model of the page (the DOM), attributes and all. Only once that model exists does the CSS engine start walking through your rules, matching selectors against parts of the DOM. So by the time &lt;code&gt;attr()&lt;/code&gt; runs, the title attribute is already sitting there on the link, waiting to be read.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To grab a named attribute — like a title on a hyperlink — here's what you need to do in your CSS:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Identify the element that has the thing you want to grab&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Point &lt;code&gt;attr()&lt;/code&gt; at that attribute&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Use it somewhere you want it to show up&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To select the prev/next links, you can use the classes Bear already supplies: &lt;code&gt;.previous-post, .next-post&lt;/code&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;So &lt;code&gt;attr(title)&lt;/code&gt; pulls the title attribute off whatever link the selector is currently pointed at. You can do the same thing with other attributes by swapping the name — &lt;code&gt;attr(href)&lt;/code&gt; will hand you the URL, to do with what you will.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Now that you have it, you can put it to work. CSS has "pseudo" elements that let you inject content before or after an element — &lt;code&gt;::before&lt;/code&gt; and &lt;code&gt;::after&lt;/code&gt; — using the &lt;code&gt;content&lt;/code&gt; property. To grab the title off these links and drop it in right after the selected element, this is all you need:&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="highlight"&gt;&lt;pre&gt;&lt;span&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="c"&gt;/* pull the title out of the DOM */&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nc"&gt;previous-post&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nd"&gt;after&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="o"&gt;,&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;span class="nt"&gt;a&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nc"&gt;next-post&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;::&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nd"&gt;after&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="w"&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;{&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;span class="w"&gt;  &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="k"&gt;content&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;:&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="w"&gt; &lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="nb"&gt;attr&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;(&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="n"&gt;title&lt;/span&gt;&lt;span class="p"&gt;);&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;span class="p"&gt;}&lt;/span&gt;
&lt;/pre&gt;&lt;/div&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And from there, style it however you like. See immediately below for what I did with it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;div class="chop"&gt;   &lt;span class="chop-letter letter-a"&gt;A&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class="chop-letter letter-b"&gt;B&lt;/span&gt;   &lt;span class="chop-letter letter-m"&gt;M&lt;/span&gt; &lt;/div&gt;

    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;i started this blog as an outlet to write about my boyfriend having cancer and it has turned into a new passion/hobby for me! while researching to make my blog, i learned of the magical world of personal websites.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i took computer science in high school to fulfill my final math credit and never looked back, it just never clicked with me - until now! i'm now building my own website and learning so much. it's been such a rewarding challenge. i'm learning html and css as i go and it's working out. i'm so excited about what i'm creating, my own online world. i feel so inspired by everything i see on neocities, bearblog, and the wider small web.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i finally have a place where i can put my thoughts into the world, and i created it!&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>https://forsomeone.bearblog.dev/are-you-a-dragonfly-now/</id>
    <title>Are you a dragonfly now?</title>
    <updated>2026-08-10T04:36:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>forsomeone</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Dear Dad,&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Hi. I miss you. It's been a few days.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After you left, a storm warning came in and the sky went from blue to gray within 30 minutes. The heavy rain was pouring down hard. I didn't even notice the changes in the sky because I was on the phone: With the hospice call line, with the nurse that just left us, with family members, with friends.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I just remember sitting on the couch next to where you always sat — scrolling through my phone and hearing the thunder crack and seeing bright flashes. I thought, man — dad's probably pissed he left.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There are so many details to the day that just went awry, if there were any warnings — I hadn't seen them except for what the nurse told me the night before about your breathing being possibly end-of-life and what your aide said that morning about your nails being bluer than usual.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I'm not ready to tell you about that day nor am I sure I'll write to you about how you left and the problems I had with the level of care you did not receive... but we'll see. The gripes are there and I'm just not sure it's the time to confront them or if it's even worth the energy when I want to pour my energy into mom getting better enough to have your viewing.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think I just wanted to tell you how much the past few days have been really weird for me. How even with death, people are not thoughtful, how moments of distraction are always welcome, how mom being sick still is worrying me because I know now she's mourning too and I think it's stopping her from getting better.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Your nieces and nephews came this weekend. Their kids left a mess in the house. They left a mess. The sink was full of dishes and you know I hate fucking washing the damn dishes. Why is your side of the family such a tornado? Lol. Thankfully G + K were here with me. They were the first ones I called when me and mom decided we should start letting people come by to say good bye to you.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;They both came Friday (they were already planning on coming — we'd been coordinating that morning but by the afternoon my last text to them was that you were gone and they both replied they were on their way), driving through the storm and traffic. They have been an immense help to me — helping wash the dishes, sitting with me while I kept myself busy. Mom is stuck in bed, Kuya is doing whatever he's doing. We're all sort of grieving how we're grieving and I called it. I said we'd all sort of just be in our own worlds for a while.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Yesterday K helped me decipher what I should prepare for your celebration of life arrangements (I decided on a viewing only because we will eventually take you back to the Philippines) and today G came over and went through the funeral home quotes with me then walked me through claiming life insurance. Both Kuya and Mom are not taking any next steps — whether it's because they don't know how or don't want to, I don't know... but I guess as usual, I have to do it all. So seriously, thank the universe for my two best friends holding my hands through this and making sure it's all getting done and that I'm doing it correctly for you.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Omg, I'm sorry dad this is going to be sucha a messy letter. I only came here because I was thinking to myself... finally, I have some time alone to do nothing but then your aide called at 10:45p to ask how you were because she didn't see you on her schedule for tomorrow.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I told her you passed away Friday afternoon and she was in shock — she said she knew you weren't doing well because of the color of your nails but that you would at least be with us for another week.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I resent that no nurse showed up on Thursday like we were told. But in the end hospice is still a business after all... and ultimately, you are now no longer suffering. I just wish we had a better warning. We were given all of 30 minutes. That is complete bullshit. BUT... let me calm down.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The point is you're no longer living how you didn't want to live in the first place. You are at peace.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;No one has left me alone since you left. It's either a text/call to check-in or a visit to see how I'm doing, then leaving a mess to clean up. After you left, Kuya immediately left to go get liquor and returned with boxes of alcohol — his friends brought pizza, the cousins brought more food. Everyone was talking and remembering and laughing... poor mom was stuck in her room coughing. Saturday was the same. Cousins came, left a mess. I had to do the dish washing in batches. I'd stop because I had to move on to the next thing. I cleared the fridge of all the food we didn't eat, all the food going bad that we cooked over the week. I collected all the garbage. I worked on the recycling. Then washed the dishes again. Both K + G are coming back again to help me clean up the real stuff. Whenever I get to that.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;At some point I remembered I started your laundry on Friday morning. It's been sitting in the washer for two days. I continued doing it today and forgot about it again.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I've been awaking up to the alarms to give you your meds. The alarms still go off for your afternoon and night meds. I just removed all the time blocks from my calendar for when I do all my caregiving tasks. I removed all the daily tasks I have to get done from my task tracker. And now I have to delete the alarms.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But I have to make new ones for mom. And add new tasks for mom. I'm not done caregiving.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Last week, mom and I started sleeping with our doors open. We are still sleeping with our doors open and saying good night to your doorway. I go in your room every morning, open the blinds, and wish you a good morning. Then at night I go in and close the blinds, then turn on the light I keep by your bedside and say good night to the air.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It's almost as if I haven't had a chance to figure out where I am yet because I'm still going through the motions only you're not here anymore. But you haven't been here for a long time and I'm wondering if that's why I'm not crying like everyone thinks I should be.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think it'll hit me later. It just all feels weird.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;30 minutes later&lt;/strong&gt;: OKAY AND SO WEIRD — I've been hearing something on my dresser (I'm sitting in the dark on my bed, writing you) and after a while, I found a giant green insect in the corner of my ceiling. I screamed (I hate bugs) and it started walking and I said... ARE YOU DAD?! And then it fell and flew around my room. I caught it and set it free after screaming for mom (lol) and I kept saying.. is it dad?! Is it dad? And she said it was a dragonfly. I don't think it was a dragonfly but dad if that was you, sorry — you know I don't like bugs! You're outside now so um... come and visit as something else later.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://forsomeone.bearblog.dev/are-you-a-dragonfly-now/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-10T04:36:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://cherrysroom.bearblog.dev/i-also-hate-fictional-ais-now/</id>
    <title>i also hate fictional AIs now</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T05:57:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>cherrysroom</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;weather:&lt;/strong&gt; ⛅ "balmy" &lt;br /&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;critters:&lt;/strong&gt; house finches&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;maybe "hate" is a strong word, but &lt;a href='https://diels-daydreams.bearblog.dev/real-ai-changed-the-way-i-see-fictional-ai/'&gt;diel's post&lt;/a&gt; enlightened me about my own shift in opinion.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i used to think of fictional AIs as characters. the narrative structures around sapient AIs usually allow and encourage this. for example, &lt;a href='https://shodan.fandom.com/wiki/SHODAN'&gt;SHODAN&lt;/a&gt;, &lt;a href='https://theportalwiki.com/wiki/GLaDOS'&gt;GLaDOS&lt;/a&gt;, and &lt;a href='https://www.marathonwiki.com/Lore:Durandal'&gt;durandal&lt;/a&gt;. these are all computers who go rogue from their programming, which is generally framed by their stories as a kind of psychotic break--except that the narrative makes them &lt;em&gt;more&lt;/em&gt; human and &lt;em&gt;more&lt;/em&gt; understandable by deviating them from their machine natures.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;i'm well aware of the distinction between the power of humanlike speech and the power of humanlike thought. every time i was too afraid to speak as a child, i was certainly thinking. but i'm more aware these days that objects may try to seem humanlike by using speech understandable to humans.&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt; people have died because their natural programming treated machine text as meaningful communication from a humanlike intelligence.&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-2"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-2"&gt;2&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;so lately i'm more inclined to think of AI characters as talking objects. even when the narrative treats them as people. maybe the stories of &lt;em&gt;portal&lt;/em&gt; and &lt;em&gt;portal 2&lt;/em&gt; will suffer for this, but hey, i already knew she wasn't really a person. she's fictional.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;i'm of the william gibson school of thought vis-à-vis the humanity of billionaires.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-2"&gt;&lt;p&gt;it strikes me as prosocial to treat an unfamiliar but communicative creature as humanlike. i don't want us to start treating this like a bug or a weakness. that tech bros exploit it to create emotional attachments to their products shouldn't be held against their victims.&lt;a href="#fnref-2" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://cherrysroom.bearblog.dev/i-also-hate-fictional-ais-now/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-08T05:57:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>

    <title>Dear Dad, thank you, i'm sorry, and I love you</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T05:34:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>forsomeone</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Dear Dad,&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You left us at 3:49p on Friday, August 7, 2026.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Me, mom, and Kuya were with you. Thank you for allowing yourself to rest, you really truly deserve it after all you've done for the people you love. Thank you for everything you've done for us. Thank you for having me. Thank you for being my dad.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I will write to you more.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I love you so much!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!&lt;br /&gt;
Chloe&lt;/p&gt;

  <entry>
    <id>https://blog.clairebot.world/cancer-changes-everything/</id>
    <title>cancer changes everything</title>
    <updated>2026-08-09T20:12:17.667949+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>clairebot</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;he's in remission but there is still grief. i mourn the life we had before cancer. i miss being carefree 20 year olds. the past year has been chemo, hospital stays, heartache, growing pains, and uncertainty. we've had to grow up so fast. the future is so much scarier than it was before. will the cancer come back? will we be able to have biological children? there is no way of knowing, and as hard as i try to accept that, the fear is still there. through therapy i've been able to come to terms with the past and the present, acceptance is such a powerful mindset. i still fear the future though. i think about going through all of this pain again and it scares me. what if i get cancer too? what if one of my parents gets cancer? anything feels possible now and that is both beautiful and terrifying. a year ago i was a completely different person. my perspectives on love, health, relationships, and life have all shifted. we've grown so much closer while going through this. we've grieved together. we've had conversations i never anticipated at this age. cancer changes everything.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://blog.clairebot.world/cancer-changes-everything/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-09T20:12:17.667949+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://annoflo.net/beginnings-and-minimal-tech/</id>
    <title>Beginnings and Minimal Tech</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T13:50:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>annoflo</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;So this is what my first blog-post will be, huh? I used to have a website where I showed my photography, sadly that turned out to be too much effort for me to enjoy. So now I am instead &lt;strong&gt;here&lt;/strong&gt;. And so far I really enjoy it, having quickly made myself a silly favicon that represents my passion for colour and light.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I have a personal dislike for social media, the only one I really used regularly since teenage-times was Reddit. But I felt like Reddit really was not good for me mentally either, so I decided to drop it. I switched to some fediverse-stuff, but just found that all of these social media concepts (excluding Pixelix) just do not do it for me. It was nice reading stuff on BlueSky, but I would rather read a proper book or an interesting article instead. That way the time would feel better-spent.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=awareness&gt;Awareness&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Eventually I also grew aware, like so many nowadays, that I use my phone more than I would really like to. That also played a part in why I wanted to cut-down on social media, but I also found the behaviour of being on my phone too much was reinforced by my Smartwatch. Having set it up to give me notifications was convenient, but also made me check my phone way too quickly. Could I have simply disabled the notifications? Of course, but that would require long-term discipline. And I wanted to make sure: So I sold the Smartwatch and got myself a good old regular analogue watch, a Tissot PRC 100 Solar to be specific. And I do not regret the choice whatsoever, even the tiny part of not having to worry about charging it is nice.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The only thing missing was the health-measurements. They are genuinely useful, especially since I have underlying health conditions. So instead I got myself one of these smart rings, and turns out: good idea, too. I never wore a ring before, but by now I am used to it and it is much less of a distraction than a smartwatch.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But then, after having gotten rid of Reddit and other stuff (with only Pixelix really left) I found that I missed reading the news. I have a personal disdain for browser bookmark management, so I decided: dust off reliable RSS and simply do it that way. And, of course, that was another great choice. Building your own feed with the things you really care about. For convenience I used Inoreader, because that way I could also access it at work.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=the-writerdeck&gt;The Writerdeck&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Writing is something I enjoy. Obviously, I guess, since I have a blog now. But creative writing is something that has been difficult for me for the past half a decade, being in something resembling a &lt;em&gt;writers block&lt;/em&gt;. I also keep my journal digitally, but my laptop and desktop have a lot of distractions on them. These things combined made it kind of difficult to actually write.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;During random research I eventually stumbled upon the term "&lt;a href='https://www.writerdeck.org/'&gt;Writerdeck&lt;/a&gt;". Summarized: It is a device which sole purpose is to write. It can take many different forms, you can buy it, you can make it yourself... Per-definition pen and paper are a writerdeck, too. I liked the idea a lot, especially since I am someone who enjoys having dedicated tech in general (I even own multiple radios to listen to music with), so I looked up what was commercially available. The results there were not particularly satisfying, with cool hardware being made a no-go for me due to needless subscriptions. &lt;em&gt;No, thank you, I do not want to pay for cloud-sync separately if I have perfectly functional cloud-storage that I already pay for.&lt;/em&gt; Therefore it was decided I would make one myself.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I found that there was an old project of a &lt;a href='https://writerdeckos.com/'&gt;writerdeck-linux-distro&lt;/a&gt;. I took that as my baseline and got myself an old ThinkPad T470 and installed it on there. It was nice, but I found it lacking and did not enjoy using tilde as a default text editor. So I got wordgrinder installed, and as seems to be customary for Linux (to my computer scientist shame I only ever dabbled with it in university and to breathe life into an old laptop for an acquaintance once), configured things for half a day. Setting up dictionaries for looking up words, translation, a basic spellchecker, being able to show the battery percentage and syncing my writing via my cloud-storage. Doing all of that was a lot of fun and I am really, really happy with the results of my writerdeck.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And, in a move that is very unlike me, I put stickers on it. I am usually a fan of keeping my equipment pristine and minimal, but with my deck it feels different. That device is now deeply personal to me, so it felt right to make it &lt;strong&gt;fully&lt;/strong&gt; mine. I find myself writing a lot more now that I have it, especially since the hurdle is a lot lower. I boot the deck and it jumps to wordgrinder, I open the file that I want to write and bam, done. Not like with my proper laptop or desktop (which are great, too!) where I need to login and have a ton of other stuff available.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=conclusions&gt;Conclusions&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;I like having minimal, dedicated stuff. I guess that is why I also like the thought of having a blog like this. I feel like this entry is way too long already, but alas. Have a cookie if you made it this far and enjoy a photo of my writerdeck with its silly stickers!
&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/annoflo/writerdeck_outside.webp" alt="Writerdeck_Outside" /&gt;
&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/annoflo/writerdeck_inside.webp" alt="Writerdeck_Inside" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://annoflo.net/beginnings-and-minimal-tech/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-08T13:50:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://blog.typewritermechanic.com/best-beginner-typewriter/</id>
    <title>forget the "best beginner" typewriter. just buy a good typewriter.</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T02:50:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>typewritermechanic</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;“What’s the best typewriter for a beginner?”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;My honest answer is that there isn’t one.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There are plenty of &lt;em&gt;bad&lt;/em&gt; first typewriters. Some are difficult to repair. Some are missing parts that are now nearly impossible to find. And others are (unfortunately, to my view) so collectible that you spend more time worrying about scratching them than actually writing. A first typewriter shouldn’t require its owner to become a museum curator.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;After buying, repairing, selling, and typing on a good many vintage machines, I’ve found myself favoring the same handful for a new owner over and over. They’re simply machines that I've found make people want to keep feeding in another sheet of paper. If there were only one quality I could choose for a typerwriter to possess, that'd be it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Here are the five I come back to most often.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=smith-corona-galaxie-series&gt;Smith-Corona Galaxie Series&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;For the writer who just wants to get words on the page.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog1.webp" alt="Blog1" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If I knew someone planned to spend all afternoon writing, there’s a good chance I’d hand them a Galaxie.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The mid-sixties Smith-Corona portables have an almost cushioned feel. They don’t beat up your fingers, and after an hour or two you stop thinking about the machine altogether. You’re just writing, which is about as high a compliment as I can give a typewriter.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;They’re wonderfully American, too. Broad, solid, optimistic machines. Typing on one feels a little like pressing the buttons that launch a Cold War missile. Somehow that’s comforting, in a "raised during the Reagan Eighties" sort of way.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;From my side of the bench, they’re equally appealing. Smith-Corona built these in huge numbers, parts are still around, and many components interchange with related machines. If one comes into my shop needing help, I’m usually optimistic before I even pick up a screwdriver.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I really feel these Smith-Corona machines present the whole package, from the beginner to the typewriter enthusiast. I'll always have at least one on hand. If you asked me for a dependable daily driver, this is where I’d begin.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=olivetti-lettera-22-32&gt;Olivetti Lettera 22 &amp; 32&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;For the hopeless romantic.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog2.webp" alt="Blog2" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;All right, now for my personal bias. I’ve tried very hard not to make every recommendation an Olivetti. But eventually honesty wins.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The Lettera 22 and 32 are my all-time favorite typewriters for simply tapping away.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;An Olympia feels crisp and authoritative. An Olivetti feels nimble. The keys dance instead of march. Everything about the experience, from the sound and the touch to the proportions and the European style, encourages you to keep going for one more paragraph.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;It’s no accident that these machines became favorites of writers and journalists. Marcello Nizzoli’s 22 design has aged so gracefully that the Lettera still looks modern on a desk, and the machines have spent decades traveling alongside everyone from Joan Didion and Leonard Cohen to Tom Hanks.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The Lettera 32, meanwhile, became famously associated with Cormac McCarthy, who saw little reason to replace it after writing much of his career on one. That’s good company, but the celebrity isn’t the point. They’re simply delightful machines to write on. Beautiful without trying too hard, and they never let their looks get in the way of being genuinely useful.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Plus, if you fall in love with the Olivetti feel but want something with a little more desktop presence, the Studio 44 is well worth exploring. It retains much of that unmistakable Olivetti character while offering a bit more substance.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=royal-quiet-de-luxe&gt;Royal Quiet De Luxe&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;For the nostalgist.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog3.webp" alt="Blog3" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If someone asked me to draw a typewriter from memory, I’d probably sketch a Royal Quiet De Luxe. To my eye, it’s what a typewriter is "supposed" to look like.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;First, it has all the right proportions. It feels substantial without being cumbersome, familiar without becoming boring, and capable without showing off.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Then there are the colors. Royal somehow pulled off a neat trick in the 1950s: it convinced people that a serious writing machine could also be turquoise, coral, seafoam green, or powder blue. The result doesn’t feel kitschy or gimmicky. It feels optimistic. Even a little punk rock.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The Quiet De Luxe also benefits from something wonderfully practical: Royal made &lt;em&gt;a lot of them&lt;/em&gt;. Parts are still obtainable, donor machines exist, and they’re straightforward to keep running.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If someone told me they’d always wanted “a vintage typewriter,” this is probably the picture they’ve had in their head all along.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=brother-charger-series&gt;Brother Charger Series&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;For the colorful modernist.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog4.webp" alt="Blog4" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Poor Brother. They rarely get invited into conversations dominated by Olympia, Hermes, and Olivetti, and I think that’s actually a real shame.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;By the 1960s, Japanese manufacturers were proving they could build machines every bit as thoughtfully engineered as their American and German competitors, typically at a friendlier price point. Brother was right in the middle of that story.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The Charger family is compact, dependable, genuinely portable, and available in enough colors to make choosing one half the fun. The orange Elite, bright yellow Charger, and red Valiant currently in my shop are three particular favorites &lt;a href='https://www.ebay.com/str/keatsandyeats'&gt;that have shown up in the store&lt;/a&gt; recently.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Buying a Brother instead of an Olympia isn’t "settling." It’s choosing a different personality... something a little lighter on its feet, a little less formal, and usually a little kinder to your wallet.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I wish more people gave them a chance.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=olympia-sm7-sm8-sm9&gt;Olympia SM7, SM8 &amp; SM9&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;For the enthusiast.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog5.webp" alt="Blog5" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If I had to choose the benchmark by which I judge most portable typewriters, it’d be the Olympia SM series.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There’s a reason they’re so respected. Everything feels deliberate. The keystroke is crisp, the controls inspire confidence, and the engineering is wonderfully German in the best possible sense of the phrase.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The SM7 uses carriage shift, while the later SM8 and SM9 use segment shift, making the Shift key noticeably lighter. It’s one of those thoughtful refinements that doesn’t change the character of the machine; it simply makes an already excellent design a little easier to live with.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Olympias often reward people who enjoy hunting for typefaces. Whether you’re after Pica, a more distinctive Elite, or one of the increasingly desirable Script machines, there are treasures to be found.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Would I recommend one to everybody? Not quite. I feel Olympias deserve to be appreciated. They aren’t machines I’d buy simply because they’re fashionable or collectible. They’re serious writing instruments, and they shine brightest in the hands of people who intend to use them that way.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If someone emailed me six months after buying an Olympia and said they’d written their first novel on it, I’d be very pleased (and not too surprised).&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=a-few-that-just-missed-the-cut&gt;A Few That Just Missed the Cut&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Limiting myself to five feels a little unfair.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;Adler Tippa S&lt;/strong&gt; remains one of the best bargains in vintage typewriters. It’s compact, thoughtfully engineered, surprisingly good to type on, and somehow still doesn’t receive the attention it deserves.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/typewritermechanic/blog6.webp" alt="Blog6" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;Smith-Corona Silent-Super&lt;/strong&gt; is another easy recommendation. If the Galaxie represents Smith-Corona’s Space Age years, the Silent-Super is mid-century America at its best: dependable, satisfying, and still capable of decades of serious writing.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And don’t overlook later &lt;strong&gt;Royal&lt;/strong&gt; portables such as the &lt;strong&gt;Royalite&lt;/strong&gt;, &lt;strong&gt;Parade&lt;/strong&gt;, and &lt;strong&gt;Safari&lt;/strong&gt;. They’re often overshadowed by their older siblings, but they can be pleasant, practical writers and are usually available without the collector premium attached to some earlier Royals.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h2 id=so-which-one-should-you-buy&gt;So... which one should you buy?&lt;/h2&gt;&lt;p&gt;Probably the one that makes you want to write.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;That’s a frustrating answer, I know, but it’s also the truth.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If comfort matters most, I’d steer you toward a Smith-Corona Galaxie. If you want something lively, elegant, and just a little romantic, it’s hard to beat an Olivetti Lettera. If you’ve always imagined owning &lt;em&gt;the&lt;/em&gt; classic American typewriter, a Royal Quiet De Luxe is a wonderful place to start.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;If you appreciate value, portability, and understated engineering, don’t sleep on a Brother. And if you’re ready to own one of the finest portable typewriters ever built, an Olympia SM will probably spoil you for everything that comes after.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;There are dozens of other machines I could have included, and on another day this list might look a little different. But the above have earned my trust.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As a mechanic, I know they’re machines I can usually keep running. As a writer, I know they’re machines that make me want to put another sheet of paper in.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To me, that’s about the highest compliment a typewriter can receive.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;(browse typewriters &lt;a href='www.ebay.com/str/keatsandyeats'&gt;here&lt;/a&gt;.)&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

    <id>https://itsme.bearblog.dev/are-search-engines-obtuse-on-purpose/</id>
    <title>Are search engines obtuse on purpose?</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T02:03:04.232602+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>itsme</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I've been trying to search for some specific information and yet it seems 'logical operators' no longer have any function in search engines. They all seem to return results based on &lt;em&gt;any&lt;/em&gt; word in your enquiry, never allowing exclusions and certainly not taking the whole entry in context.&lt;br /&gt;
As such I'm speculating the idea is to make standard search engines so functionally useless as to force people into using data-harvesting AI garbage searches in order to train the LLM and of course glean as much personal information they can sell as possible.&lt;br /&gt;
Getting more than just a little sick of this "technology is your master" ideology.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>

  <entry>
    <id>https://magmacranes.bearblog.dev/one-of-the-least-interesting-things-about-me/</id>
    <title>One of the least interesting things about me</title>
    <updated>2026-08-10T02:56:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>magmacranes</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;Since this is my first post in awhile, I could tell you about how for the past few months I’ve been having a lot more of these episodes.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Episodes where my ears are full of cotton and my head is floating away and my heart has decided to take up tap dancing and my legs just won’t stop shaking.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I could tell you about ice packs and doctor appointments and electrolytes and all the things I’ve missed out on this summer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But that’s honestly one of the least interesting things about me.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;What’s more interesting is that I’m scoring a film with a wind quintet and I think the flute is like raindrops falling on pebbles and the clarinet is like rustling leaves and the oboe is like rich soil and the horn is like granite boulders and the bassoon is like the sturdy trunks of centuries-old trees.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And that I recently made strawberry syrup to put on my ice cream and now I don’t understand why I ever wasted money buying bottles of it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And I usually don’t like musicals, but I absolutely loved Hadestown. It was one of those rare moments where I think experiencing a work of art may have actually changed me as a person a bit.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And my favorite part of most days are evenings spent watching cooking competition TV shows with my husband and two cats.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I want to visit Iceland.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I want to write more synth music.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I want to be a more thoughtful friend.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I want to start journaling again.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;These things are all more interesting than those first things.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;You understand, right?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I think I’ve had a chronic illness for a long time without knowing it. But now that I know, I tend to get very down during flare-ups. Lamenting the unfairness of it, thoughts threatening to veer into self-loathing.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;But no.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’ve found that when I remind myself that this is one of the least interesting things about me, it always snaps me out of it. I hate anything that’s boring.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And even if I’m feeling awful and can’t do much,&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I can always listen to a podcast about scammers&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Or read a library book&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Or pull some tarot cards&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Or picture myself floating on my back in Lake Michigan&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Or look at the way the sunlight is streaming in through the blinds.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://magmacranes.bearblog.dev/one-of-the-least-interesting-things-about-me/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-10T02:56:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://householderkarl.com/if-buying-isnt-owning/</id>
    <title>If Buying Isn't Owning</title>
    <updated>2026-08-07T22:06:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>householderkarl</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/householderkarl/image-11.webp#center" alt="image" /&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p align="center"&gt;&lt;sup&gt;&lt;small&gt;The good old days&lt;/small&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=piracy-isnt-stealing&gt;Piracy isn’t stealing.&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;I’ve been seeing this a lot lately, mostly in response to the rising consumer frustration with digital rights management (DRM) and the proliferation of sketchy subscription models. It raises some interesting moral questions about the nature of ownership.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I never read the EULA, but from what I’ve gathered, when we purchase digital media we are receiving a license to access the content, not the content itself. The license is revocable; companies often delist games, shut down servers, etc. This sounds more like “renting” than “purchasing”, but the distinction isn’t made clear to the average consumer.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And that’s where I have a problem, I think. If I’m essentially renting a game, why should I pay the same price I used to pay for physical media? If a game disc costs $80, why should a revocable digital license cost the same or more?&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;In this example, I’m willing to accept the $80 as an “ownership premium”. That game is mine forever. I’m &lt;em&gt;free&lt;/em&gt; to play it whenever I choose. In the current model, with revocable licenses, I’m paying the same for less. My relationship to the media is now dictated by someone else.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I would argue that &lt;em&gt;ownership&lt;/em&gt; has value. It’s more than mere possession; it represents freedom of choice. If I pay the price, I should retain that freedom. If they want to formally establish a rental system, the price needs to be adjusted accordingly. We already have something like that with XBOX Game Pass.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;As the quote suggests, one alternative is to sail the digital high seas. But is this morally &lt;em&gt;wrong&lt;/em&gt;? I think the answer requires more nuance than just a simple &lt;em&gt;yes&lt;/em&gt; or &lt;em&gt;no&lt;/em&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Trust is a two-way street. If publishers want consumers to respect intellectual property laws, they must respect the basic expectation of purchase permanency. When “buying” loses its meaning, “stealing” loses its moral weight. Personally, my first reaction is, “Screw me!? No, screw you!” And thus the guilt quickly fades as I fire up the VPN and search for a torrent.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;I’m not saying that the solution is to &lt;em&gt;normalize&lt;/em&gt; piracy, nor is it to accept arbitrary server shutdowns. The solution is demanding regulatory transparency. If a purchase is just a rental, consumer protection laws should require it to be labeled and priced as one.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The way I see it today, when these publishers charge full price for digital media, but then revoke access later, they are breaking the unwritten covenant of fair trade, regardless of what the EULA might say.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;h3 id=you-didnt-answer-the-question-karl&gt;You didn’t answer the question, Karl.&lt;/h3&gt;&lt;p&gt;I know. I still don’t know if it’s right or wrong. I'm not even sure it's a valid question. My gut says, “Stealing is always wrong. Support DRM-free platforms or just don’t play games.” But then my Tricorne-wearing, black flag-flying side says, “They’re stealing from YOU, Karl! They abuse their artists and pocket incredible wealth! Fair winds and following seas!”&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Perhaps I’m stuck in a false dichotomy here. Maybe everything is on fire and we should just do as we please.&lt;/p&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://householderkarl.com/if-buying-isnt-owning/" rel="alternate"/>
    <published>2026-08-07T22:06:00+00:00</published>
  </entry>
  <entry>
    <id>https://notes.jeddacp.com/we-the-people-matter/</id>
    <title>We The People Matter</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T01:38:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>jedda</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;I haven't been inspired to post on &lt;a href='https://jeddacp.me/'&gt;august morning&lt;/a&gt; for quite some time now, even though I have a bit of a backlog of photos I &lt;em&gt;would&lt;/em&gt; like to share one day&lt;sup class="footnote-ref" id="fnref-1"&gt;&lt;a href="#fn-1"&gt;1&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/sup&gt;. Recently, I came across Inventory Full's Blaugust &lt;a href='https://bhagpuss.blogspot.com/2025/08/so-long-blaugust-and-thanks-for-all.html'&gt;Class of 2025&lt;/a&gt; post again, where my photo blog was mentioned. It reminded me that I do, in fact, miss sharing some of my just &lt;em&gt;day to day&lt;/em&gt; photos. Maybe until I'm ready to commit to posting on august morning again, I can share a few photos here occasionally instead.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;img src="https://bear-images.sfo2.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/jedda/wethepeoplematter.png" alt="A sign that says We The People Matter in front of a window" /&gt;
&lt;small&gt;This photo is from a visit to Guerneville, CA last week. We were barely in town for an hour, but that's a story for another time.&lt;/small&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;section class="footnotes"&gt;
&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li id="fn-1"&gt;&lt;p&gt;Like part 3 of my &lt;a href='https://jeddacp.me/shineforthbeauty/'&gt;San Francisco Elopement series&lt;/a&gt; that I never got to post.&lt;a href="#fnref-1" class="footnote"&gt;&amp;#8617;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;
&lt;/section&gt;
</content>
    <link href="https://notes.jeddacp.com/we-the-people-matter/" rel="alternate"/>

  <entry>
    <id>https://fldigitalrights.org/rally-against-flock-cameras-in-melbourne-fl/</id>
    <title>Rally against Flock cameras in Melbourne, FL - Aug 19</title>
    <updated>2026-08-08T01:20:00+00:00</updated>
    <author>
      <name>fldigitalrights</name>
      <email>hidden</email>
    </author>
    <content type="html">&lt;p&gt;By &lt;strong&gt;FLDR Brevard&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Join us as we show our community that Flock and other mass surveillance cameras are not welcome here! We know how these cameras work, &lt;a href='https://www.fldigitalrights.org/the-state-of-flock-surveillance-in-florida/'&gt;we know how big the problem is&lt;/a&gt;, and we're not having it.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;We will be demonstrating against automated license plate readers and passing out flyers with more information, joining groups &lt;a href='https://noalprs.com' target='_blank'&gt;across the country for the DeFlock National Week of Action&lt;/a&gt;. Flock erodes our right to privacy and does not make our communities safer. People ought to know!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sign Waive and Flyer Handout&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Date: Wednesday, August 19&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Time: 4:00 PM - 5:30 PM&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Location: Melbourne, FL (exact location TBA)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;
&lt;p&gt;To learn the location of the rally when it's announced, enter our &lt;a href='https://www.fldigitalrights.org/signal/' target='_blank'&gt;Signal group chat&lt;/a&gt;, follow us on &lt;a href='https://bsky.app/profile/fldigitalrights.org' target='_blank'&gt;Bluesky&lt;/a&gt; and &lt;a href='https://defcon.social/@fldigitalrights' target='_blank'&gt;Mastodon&lt;/a&gt;, or come back to this webpage closer to the event. We're excited to see you there!&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;hr /&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Follow us on &lt;a href='https://bsky.app/profile/fldigitalrights.org' target='_blank'&gt;Bluesky&lt;/a&gt; and &lt;a href='https://defcon.social/@fldigitalrights' target='_blank'&gt;Mastodon&lt;/a&gt;. Share your thoughts on this blog post!&lt;/p&gt;
